source_title: Current correctional and local detention facility UAS buffers and infrastructure exception
revision_date: Repeal scheduled January 1, 2027 by 2026 Act No. 150
uas_topic: Correctional facilities; detention facilities; notice; infrastructure
regulated_party: Any UAS operator near a state correctional or local detention facility
regulated_activity: Operating within 500 feet horizontally or 250 feet vertically of a covered facility
requirement_type: Written-consent rule with commercial infrastructure notification exception and confiscation exposure
permit_or_approval_required: Written consent, or qualifying notification no more than five days and no less than two hours before each operation
summary: Through December 31, 2026, South Carolina prohibits UAS operation within 500 feet horizontally or 250 feet vertically of a Department of Corrections facility or local detention facility without written consent from the Corrections Director or jail administrator. A federally registered commercial operator is excepted when monitoring, operating, maintaining, enhancing, or assessing repairs to electric, communications, water-conveyance, or transportation infrastructure, but must notify the appropriate official separately for each operation no more than five days and no less than two hours beforehand and provide the FAA registration number. Violations may lead to misdemeanor penalties and aircraft confiscation.
notes: The local-facility text is at https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t24c005.php. Both sections are repealed when Act 150 takes effect January 1, 2027.

geographic_scope: South Carolina correctional and detention facilities
issuing_authority: South Carolina General Assembly and South Carolina Aeronautics Commission
source_title: Correctional facility boundary and FAA fixed-site publication duties
uas_topic: Correctional facilities; boundary mapping; FAA fixed-site restrictions
regulated_party: South Carolina Department of Corrections, local detention facilities, and South Carolina Aeronautics Commission
regulated_activity: Petitioning for federal fixed-site restrictions and publishing facility boundaries
requirement_type: Agency petition, data-submission, and publication requirements
permit_or_approval_required: No operator permit created; operators use the published boundary information for planning
summary: The Department of Corrections must petition the FAA to designate qualifying detention and correctional facilities as fixed-site facilities, and the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission must publish FAA designations. Corrections and local detention facilities also must provide site lists and electronic UAS-boundary data to the Commission for publication in its GIS. The Commission currently provides an SCDOC UAV No Fly Zone Map and identifies SCDOC as the data owner. These mapping duties support flight planning but do not replace the operator obligation to apply the governing statutory distance, obtain required permission or notice, and check current FAA restrictions.
notes: Act 150 repeals §§ 24-1-300 and 24-5-175 on January 1, 2027 but does not expressly repeal §§ 24-1-310 and 24-1-320.

source_title: Act 150 federal compliance, registration, and controlled-airspace offenses
uas_topic: Federal compliance; controlled airspace; registration; penalties
regulated_activity: Operating, taking off, or landing a drone in South Carolina
requirement_type: State enforcement of specified federal-compliance and registration duties
permit_or_approval_required: FAA authorization is required when applicable; no separate general state commercial permit is created
summary: Beginning January 1, 2027, Act 150 requires compliance with applicable FAA registration, operating, airspace, waiver, exemption, and authorization requirements and states that South Carolina does not supersede federal airspace authority. It creates state misdemeanors for intentionally or knowingly operating, taking off, or landing in FAA-designated controlled airspace without required authorization and for specified knowing registration violations, including unregistered commercial operation. Penalties escalate for repeat offenses, and each violated subsection or provision is a separate offense. The act defines a commercial operator by business-purpose operation in compliance with FAA rules but does not create a separate state commercial license.
notes: This record is prospective. Existing law remains controlling until the January 1, 2027 effective date.

source_title: Act 150 correctional, detention, and military facility 1,500-foot restrictions
uas_topic: Correctional facilities; detention facilities; military installations; written consent
regulated_party: Any UAS operator near a covered facility
regulated_activity: Intentionally or knowingly operating, taking off, or landing directly above or within 1,500 feet horizontally of a covered property boundary
requirement_type: Written-consent rule and escalating misdemeanor penalties
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — express written facility authorization or consent; official-duty facility personnel are excepted
summary: On January 1, 2027, Act 150 replaces the current correctional statutes with a prohibition on intentionally or knowingly operating, taking off, or landing directly above or within 1,500 feet horizontally of a known federal, state, county, or municipal correctional or detention facility unless the appropriate corrections or governing authority gives express written authorization or consent. The same 1,500-foot rule applies to a known military installation without prior express written consent from the Department of Defense or installation commander. The act excepts facility or military personnel acting within official duties, but does not carry forward the current commercial infrastructure notification exception.
notes: The distance is measured horizontally from the outermost property boundary. Mission planning must account for the changed distance and exception structure before January 1, 2027 work.

source_title: Act 150 contraband, malicious facility surveillance, weaponization, and seizure provisions
uas_topic: Contraband; malicious surveillance; mapping; thermal and geospatial data; weaponization; seizure
regulated_party: Any person operating, taking off, landing, or possessing a drone with prohibited intent
regulated_activity: Contraband delivery, malicious facility data collection, weaponization, threats, or harm
requirement_type: Felony prohibitions, aircraft seizure, and separate-offense treatment
summary: Beginning January 1, 2027, Act 150 creates felony offenses for operating, taking off, landing, or possessing a drone with intent to deliver contraband to a correctional or detention facility; collect visual, photographic, video, geospatial, thermal, or other sensory information about a military or correctional facility to identify vulnerabilities or for another unlawful purpose; or weaponize the drone or threaten or harm persons or property. Aircraft involved may be seized, retained, transferred, or destroyed after proceedings, subject to an innocent-owner process. The data-collection offense requires the stated malicious or unlawful intent; it is not a general ban on every map or image.

source_title: Act 150 state-local regulatory boundary for public-property operations
uas_topic: State preemption; local authority; public property; takeoff and landing sites
regulated_party: Municipalities, counties, other political subdivisions, and UAS operators
regulated_activity: Local regulation of drone takeoff, landing, and operation on or above public property
requirement_type: Conflict preemption with preserved local public-property authority
permit_or_approval_required: Local permission may be required for public-property use under a consistent local rule
summary: Effective January 1, 2027, a South Carolina municipality, county, or other political subdivision may not enact an ordinance that conflicts with Article 3 or FAA regulations. The act nevertheless preserves local authority to impose reasonable restrictions on drone takeoff and landing sites and on operation on or above public property within the jurisdiction when the subject is not otherwise covered by the article. This is conflict preemption rather than a complete displacement of local UAS rules. Local public-property permission and operating restrictions may therefore remain material even after the statewide act becomes effective.
notes: Local ordinance research is deferred under current project scope. This record reports only the state-level allocation of authority.

geographic_scope: Professional engineering, surveying, and photogrammetric practice in South Carolina
issuing_authority: South Carolina Board of Registration for Professional Engineers and Surveyors
source_title: Professional board policy on UAV scanning, LiDAR, and photogrammetric surveying
citation: S.C. Board of Registration for Professional Engineers and Surveyors, UAV Policy (2017); Board Minutes (Jan. 15, 2019)
revision_date: Clarified January 15, 2019; current policy page reviewed 2026-08-02
uas_topic: Professional licensing; surveying; photogrammetry; LiDAR; mapping
regulated_party: AEC firms and professionals producing survey or photogrammetric deliverables from UAV data
regulated_activity: UAV scanning, LiDAR, mapping, photography, and photogrammetric surveying
permit_or_approval_required: Professional licensure is required when the work constitutes regulated surveying or photogrammetry; the drone itself is not licensed by the Board
summary: The South Carolina engineering and surveying board states that it regulates professional practice, not drones or other tools, and recognizes scanning, LiDAR, and similar UAV methods as acceptable techniques for Tier A or Tier B surveying. In later official minutes, the Board distinguished taking a photograph from photogrammetry and explained that creating measured, overlapping-image products such as contours constitutes licensed photogrammetric practice. The operator credential and the professional credential therefore address different functions: using a drone does not itself require a Board license, but offering or producing regulated survey or photogrammetric work must be performed within the applicable professional-licensure framework.
notes: The 2019 minutes are at https://llr.sc.gov/eng/Minutes/Minutes%20-%20January%2015%2C%202019.pdf. Project scope and deliverable use determine the professional-practice classification.

issuing_authority: South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism and South Carolina Film Commission
source_title: State park drone coordination and commercial filming permit requirements
citation: South Carolina State Parks FAQ; South Carolina Film Commission Permits guidance
uas_topic: State parks; commercial filming; photography; insurance
regulated_party: Commercial drone operators and productions using state-owned parks
regulated_activity: Bringing or operating a drone in a state park and performing commercial aerial filming or photography
requirement_type: Advance park coordination and filming permit conditions
permit_or_approval_required: Yes for commercial filming; contact the specific park and the state park operations contact
summary: South Carolina State Parks directs anyone seeking to bring a drone to a state park to contact that park directly. The South Carolina Film Commission identifies a permit contact for filming within state-owned parks and expressly reminds commercial aerial-drone operators of Part 107 requirements. Its production permit guidance requires an original certificate of insurance, at least one million dollars in liability coverage, naming the State and its agents as additional insured, and indemnification of the State. Because the public FAQ does not publish a uniform drone approval form or processing time, location-specific authorization and operating conditions must be confirmed before mobilization.
notes: The state-parks drone FAQ is at https://southcarolinaparks.com/faqs. The Film Commission guidance addresses production permits; a park may apply additional resource, visitor, or location conditions.

geographic_scope: Federally funded SCDOT and local public agency projects or grants using the required provisions
source_title: SCDOT federally funded project restriction on covered foreign UAS
citation: SCDOT LPA Required Provisions, Special Provision to Section 107 (2025)
binding_level: Contractual requirement for covered federally funded projects and grants
uas_topic: Procurement; covered foreign entities; federally funded transportation projects; data processing
regulated_party: Contractors and subrecipients performing covered SCDOT or local public agency work
regulated_activity: Purchasing or using UAS, maintaining UAS fleets, and processing UAS data on federally funded projects or grants
requirement_type: Prohibition on covered foreign UAS use and purchase with federal funds
permit_or_approval_required: No; equipment and service compliance must be established through project procurement and contract administration
public_agency_only: Yes — applies through covered federally funded public projects and grants
summary: SCDOT Local Public Agency required provisions implement the American Security Drone Act and OMB Memorandum M-26-02 for federally funded work. The special provision directs contractors to refrain from purchasing or using UAS manufactured by covered foreign entities within existing fleets for operations, maintenance, or data processing on any federally funded project or grant. It points to the Federal Acquisition Security Council list on SAM.gov and a cleared-drone list. This is a project-funding and contract rule rather than a statewide ban on private commercial ownership, but it can disqualify aircraft, associated services, or processing workflows proposed for covered transportation work.
notes: The incorporated federal covered-entity list can change. The current solicitation, funding source, and contract clauses control; no named product is declared compliant by this record.
